{"rule":"Return this JSON object with the rule field unchanged and a new passage of about 250 words in the text field.","text":"Every morning, Mara wound the clock in the village library. It had stopped years before she took the job, but the librarian insisted the winding kept dust out of its gears. Mara liked the small ritual, so she never argued.

One rainy morning, the clock struck nine while she was holding the key. Its hands still pointed to six.

The librarian looked up from his desk. “That’s new,” he said.

At nine that evening, the clock struck again. Mara had stayed late to repair a torn atlas. She counted twelve chimes this time, then watched the minute hand creep backward until it pointed to half past three.

There was a newspaper from thirty years ago open on the desk beside her. At half past three, according to its front page, a flood had reached the library steps.

Mara climbed down to the basement. Water was seeping through a crack in the wall, gathering around the lowest shelves. She called the librarian, and together they carried the archive upstairs. By midnight, the basement floor was under an inch of water.

A plumber found a broken pipe beneath the street the next day. Nothing in the archive had been damaged.

On Monday, Mara wound the clock as usual. Its hands had returned to six. She waited, but it made no sound.

The librarian brought her a cup of tea. “My grandmother used to wind it,” he said. “She always claimed it was better at remembering than telling time.”

Mara set down the key and listened. Behind the steady rain at the windows, the clock gave one quiet tick."}
